S1.1: What are the main standard library approaches for handling multiple TCP connections in Python?
  E11 (docs.python.org): "asyncio offers an alternative approach to achieving task level
concurrency without requiring the use of multiple operating system threads"
S1.2: What are the performance and complexity trade-offs between threading and selectors for 10+ clients?
  E1 (docs.python.org): "CPython implementation detail: In CPython, due to the Global Interpreter Lock, only one thread
can execute Python code at once (even though certain performance-oriented
libraries might overcome this limitation)"
  E2 (docs.python.org): "However, threading is still an appropriate model if you want to run
multiple I/O-bound tasks simultaneously"
  E3 (docs.python.org): "This should be the default choice for most users"
  E6 (docs.python.org): "This module allows high-level and efficient I/O multiplexing, built upon the
select module primitives. Users are encouraged to use this module
instead, unless they want precise control over the OS-level primitives used"
  E7 (docs.python.org): "conn.setblocking(False)
    sel.register(conn, selectors.EVENT_READ, read)"
  E12 (docs.python.org): "However, the GIL limits the performance gains of threading when it comes to
CPU-bound tasks, as only one thread can execute Python bytecode at a time"
S1.3: What are common pitfalls when implementing concurrent TCP servers in Python?
  E8 (docs.python.org): "concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor offers a higher level interface
to push tasks to a background thread without blocking execution of the
calling thread, while still being able to retrieve their results when needed"
S2.1: How can unique nicknames be enforced in a multi-threaded Python server?
  E4 (docs.python.org): "queue provides a thread-safe interface for exchanging data between
running threads"
S2.2: What are the race conditions associated with checking and setting user state in threads?
  E5 (docs.python.org): "These two constants, if defined, can be combined with the socket types and allow you to set some flags atomically (thus avoiding possible race conditions and the need for separate calls)"
  E9 (docs.python.org): "A primitive lock is a synchronization primitive that is not owned by a
particular thread when locked.  In Python, it is currently the lowest level
synchronization primitive available, implemented directly by the _thread
extension module"
S3.2: How to structure commands like /msg within a text-based chat protocol?
  E10 (docs.python.org): "Assuming you don’t want to end the connection, the simplest solution is a fixed length message"
